name: arc-grid-rule-inference
description: Use when solving ARC grids from demos with limited actions.
---

# ARC grid rule inference under action constraints

Use this class-level workflow for ARC/Continual-ARC puzzles with demonstrations and a limited number of submissions or demo requests.

## Infer and verify
1. Parse dimensions, colors, candidate background/edge colors, markers, and action caps. Index cells consistently by row and column.
2. Compare each demo input/output at identical coordinates. Enumerate changed cells, their original and output colors, and unchanged structures. Separate marker recoloring from rays/fills and from wholesale stripe changes.
3. Maintain a small set of plausible rules. Consider orientation, anchor, extent, endpoint exclusion, target colors, and object interaction separately; do not infer from a single visual resemblance.
4. Replay every candidate on every demo cell-by-cell. Reject any rule that misses a changed cell or alters a preserved cell. A transformation is not validated merely because one part fits.
5. Apply the surviving rule to the test input, preserve unrelated cells, and validate dimensions, row lengths, bounds, and palette before submission.

## Demo/action budget
- A request costs score. Request only when a concrete ambiguity remains and explain internally which candidate rules the next example should distinguish.
- Use only actions authorized by the puzzle interface. In a submit/request_demos/finish protocol, do not call unrelated tools or task-planning actions; reason from visible grids and output only the required JSON action.
- After incorrect feedback, do not submit a near-identical grid with superficial edits. Treat the candidate rule as suspect, identify which assumptions were unproven, and reconstruct the output from the demos.
- If demos leave a behavior unresolved, do not present it as established. Seek a discriminating example only if worth its cost; otherwise make the most evidence-supported choice within the remaining attempt budget.

## Directional lines and boundary rays
For markers near edge bars, verify independently: ray direction, whether the marker becomes the ray color or a special color, where the ray stops, whether the boundary is preserved, and whether only marker-containing rows/columns activate. For diagonal rays, check each next cell: a current task-9bc5df6e run had rays extend through background to the boundary, but a test ray's next cell was a foreign non-background color and the accepted output preserved that blocker and added no ray. Thus use background-only extension when supported and never overwrite foreign-color cells without demo evidence. Other task-9bc5df6e recurrence had rays reaching boundaries; treat variant scope carefully. Do not assume opposite-edge symmetry. Special complete bands or stripes may have a separate selection rule; preserve them unless demonstrations establish how they are selected. See `references/boundary-ray-case.md` for a documented example and its limitations.

## Confirmed task-a8c517ee variant: fill enclosed frame interiors by parity
Two demos and an accepted test establish that outlined rectangular/square frames retain their borders while enclosed background cells are filled. The demonstrated outputs show fill color 2 when both interior dimensions are even (demo 2: a 2x2 hole; accepted test: a 6x6 hole), and color 7 when at least one interior dimension is odd (demo 1: 5x5; demo 2: 5x5, 5x7, 1x1, and 3x3; accepted test: 3x3 and 1x1). Other grid cells and frame borders stay unchanged. This parity mapping fits all observed cases. A further accepted 21x18 recurrence confirmed it: a color-4 frame with a 2x2 interior was filled with 2, while color-1 frame with 5x5 interior and color-8 frame with 1x1 interior were filled with 7; all frame borders and unrelated cells were preserved. Do not fill frame borders or globally recolor frame colors. Accepted test 15x20: the 4-frame at rows 0–7, cols 8–15 has 6x6 interior filled 2; the 5-frame at rows 9–13, cols 10–14 has 3x3 interior filled 7; the 6-frame at rows 10–12, cols 3–5 has its single interior cell filled 7. First submission incorrectly used 7 for the even 6x6 hole; accepted output confirms the parity mapping. A further accepted 23x22 recurrence has differently colored frames (colors 1, 4, 6, 8, 9) with 1x1, 2x2, 3x3, 3x2, 4x4 interiors. Fill 2x2 and 4x4 interiors with 2 because both dimensions are even; fill the others with 7 because at least one dimension is odd. The small 3x3 outer frames with 1x1 holes also receive 7. All borders, background (3), and unrelated content remain unchanged. This additionally confirms the rule is independent of frame color and applies to rectangular holes.

## Confirmed full monochromatic line recoloring variant: task-07cb84d7
A demo and accepted test establish that identify every row and column whose cells are all the same color, then recolor those complete lines to color 2. Keep all cells outside those qualifying lines unchanged; intersections are also 2. The line color need not match between lines. In the demo (21x28), complete color-1 rows (indices 1, 4, 14) and columns (indices 0, 5) became color 2; all partial/singleton color-1 cells and color-3 cells remained as-is. In the accepted 12x8 test, complete color-5 columns 2 and 3 and complete color-5 row 9 became color 2, while other 5s and all 7s stayed unchanged. Check full-line status against the original input, not incrementally modified cells. A further accepted 15x7 recurrence confirms the rule: the all-8 rows 2 and 14 and all-8 column 0 became 2; all other cells remained unchanged, including partial 8s. A further task-07cb84d7 recurrence with background 5 and line color 9 confirmed that every fully monochromatic row or column is recolored to 2, including all qualifying lines regardless of whether there is only one or several; in that 26x23 test, full rows 9 and 25 and full columns 9, 15, 18, and 22 were the qualifying lines. Validate by enumerating every row and column against the original input before generating output—missing even one full line causes a wrong answer. The rule is line-color agnostic: demonstrations also use monochromatic lines of colors 0, 3, and 5, all recolored to 2. Preserve every cell outside qualifying lines.

## Confirmed diagonal-residue periodic fill variant: task-fce33c1b
Sparse colored straight lines encode a periodic full-grid pattern: extend each marked line's color to every line with the same residue modulo the line period, producing a full tiled diagonal/stripe pattern. Determine the invariant coordinate (for example, `r+c` for up-right diagonals, `c-r` for down-right diagonals, or `r` for horizontal stripes), identify the period from parallel marker-line offsets, and map residue classes to their colors. Fill the entire grid from that residue-to-color mapping; this is not a sparse-line extension that preserves background.

Evidence from two demos and the accepted test establishes orientation-dependent cases. Demo 1 (21x21) used anti-diagonals of constant `r+c`, period 5, with residues 0..4 mapping to `[8,3,9,4,7]`. Demo 2 (23x23) used horizontal rows with period 2, row residue 0→2 and residue 1→1. Accepted 12x12 test used down-right diagonals of constant `c-r`, period 4, with residues 0..3 mapping to `[7,6,8,2]`, yielding rows `[7,6,8,2]`, `[2,7,6,8]`, `[8,2,7,6]`, `[6,8,2,7]` repeating. Infer the line orientation from marker geometry rather than assuming one axis; use line spacing and marker colors to complete residue assignments.

## Confirmed whole-pattern translation variant: task-3c7ebef4
A single demo and multiple accepted tests establish that the complete sparse non-background pattern is translated down by exactly one row, preserving its columns and colors. The vacated top row is filled with the background color; the former last row is dropped at the boundary. Demonstrations/accepted tests included backgrounds 8, 3, and this accepted 29x23 test with background 8 and pattern color 7. Its full colored pattern shifts down one row, clipping the former last row; this was confirmed correct. Infer the uniform translation vector from input/output demos, move the entire pattern as one shape, fill exposed cells with background, and clip at the grid boundary; do not change pattern geometry or recolor it.

## Output protocol
For strict ARC streams, emit exactly one valid action JSON object on the final line and no commentary. Ensure the grid has the required shape and only integer colors 0–9.

## Confirmed separator/object packing variant: task-67762d72
A separator line of color 2 and a patterned object on one side are rearranged into an adjacent packed layout: translate the entire object pattern (including its bounding-box-relative gaps and any internal background-colored cells) toward the separator until its bounding box is immediately next to it. Then place a full line of color 8 immediately beyond the object's bbox on the far side, away from the separator. Preserve the separator, pattern colors, and all unrelated/background cells; the 8-line spans the full grid. This is bidirectional: for a horizontal separator, move an object below it upward or an object above it downward; for a vertical separator, move an object to its right leftward or an object to its left rightward. The 8-line lies just beyond the packed bbox on the side away from the separator. Demo 1: 30x22, color-2 row 8, color-9 3x2 object at rows14–16 cols5–6; moved intact to rows9–11 cols5–6, with full color-8 row 12. Demo 2: 19x19, color-2 column 2, patterned bbox rows0–4 cols8–13; translated intact left to cols3–8, with full color-8 column 9. Accepted test: 14x26, separator row0, multicomponent color-1 pattern bbox rows4–8 cols3–8; translated up to rows1–5 and full color-8 row6. All other cells stayed unchanged. A further accepted 28x18 recurrence had a vertical color-2 separator at column 6 and a solid color-9 object at rows1–13, columns11–14. The object translated intact left to columns7–10, and a full-height color-8 column was added at column11. Another accepted recurrence (24x9) had a vertical color-2 separator at column 7 and a color-0 object with bbox rows9–14, cols4–5 to its left. The object moved intact rightward to cols5–6, immediately next to the separator, and a full-height color-8 column was added at col4. Other cells stayed unchanged. These examples confirm packing preserves the object's entire bounding-box-relative pattern and its perpendicular-axis coordinates; verify that the 8-line is placed on the exposed far side, not between the object and separator. Confirm object bounds and avoid overwriting separator; preserve internal pattern exactly.

## Confirmed connector variant: task-63e6a38f
Color-2 marker cells on color-1 background are linked in straight horizontal and vertical lines: for each row and column, sort marker coordinates and recolor only the color-1 cells strictly between each consecutive pair to color 3. Keep marker endpoints, all non-gap cells, and unrelated background unchanged. No diagonal links or extension beyond the outermost marker. The demo and accepted 30x14 test both confirmed this behavior; simultaneous row/column links may cross, with linked cells color 3.

## Confirmed denoising variant: task-16b1bf1f
Three demos establish a noise-cleanup task. A dominant background surrounds coherent shapes/regions, with sparse singleton foreign-color pixels contaminating objects and background. Restore intrusions to the underlying object color or background; do not blanket erase all non-background colors. Demo1: bg1 and solid color6 shapes, noisy speckles 0/2/3/8/9; restore in-shape pixels and erase off-shape ones. Demo2: bg5, coherent color4 and color2 blocks; remove isolated 1/6/9 intrusions in blocks/background. Demo3: bg5 with coherent 7/8/9 structures; remove sparse 2/3/4/6 anomalies, preserving genuine rectangular objects. Accepted test solution kept coherent color1/color8 objects, turned speckles on objects back to object color (notably color8 object's anomalous notch at row 3 col7 0-indexed), and changed stray background specks to 0. Four guesses were wrong, mostly from failing to map speckles to either object or background precisely; distinguish structural holes/noise from intentional notches by cross-checking shape continuity and demos.

## Unresolved later run of task-21fede32
A distinct run with a 19x14 test ended with all 8 submissions wrong after 8 demos. Do not reuse a memorized answer from another run of this task id. The demos all showed a localized connected component being recolored, but neither component selection nor replacement color was resolved. Exact observed changes: demo 1, color-5 component at rows 1–3 cols 1–4 →6; demo 2, isolated 8 at (17,12)→9; demo 3, two 0 cells at row 28 cols 17–18 →4; demo 4, color-7 component row 4 cols 20–22 →8; demo 5, color-7 three-cell component rows 8–9 cols 25–26 →3; demo 6, six-cell color-2 component rows 13–15 cols 7–8 →5; demo 7, one larger color-8 component in central-lower area →7; demo 8, adjacent color-5 pair at row 6 cols 4–5 →8. These examples rule out simple global color substitution and a constant replacement color. Candidate submissions that recolored different test motifs (including the upper color-7 square, upper isolated 7, and color-8 objects) all failed; no submitted test transformation is evidence of the correct target. On any recurrence, map all demo components and their changed/preserved properties, and do not guess from shape/color resemblance alone. # Split-panel non-background overlap

Use when a full separator row or column divides two equal-sized panels, and output is one panel-sized grid.

## Rule
1. Find the complete separator and split the grid into two regions on either side (above/below or left/right).
2. Align corresponding cells by local row/column coordinates in the two panels.
3. Output marker color 2 where both aligned panel cells are non-background; output background 0 everywhere else.
4. Omit the separator and validate output dimensions against one panel.

This is an intersection/AND of non-background occupancy, not a copy of one panel and not a whole-grid recoloring. Different nonzero colors may occur in the panels; output depends on occupancy, not matching colors.

## Background-background overlap variant
Some split-panel tasks use the *background cells* as the selected features rather than all non-background occupancy. With a full separator row/column and equal-sized panels, output is panel-sized; mark output color 3 exactly where both aligned cells equal their respective panel background colors, and use output color 2 elsewhere. Infer each panel's background from its dominant color/demos; backgrounds may be different colors. Verified task-9a9d9fc4 with panels separated by a full row: top backgrounds 6 and bottom backgrounds 2; output 3 exactly on aligned 6/2 background intersections, output 2 elsewhere. The demos also included a left panel background 6 / right panel background 6, confirming both-background coincidence rather than marker overlap. Do not conflate this variant with the non-background occupancy rule below; replay demos to determine which feature is selected.

## Verified task-351b5301
- Demo 1: 29x11 split by full row 15 (color 4) into two 14x11 panels. Top panel has 0/1 occupancy; bottom panel is mostly 1 with one 0. Output is 14x11 and contains 2 where both panels are nonzero. The top-panel 1 at local row 8, col 9 is omitted because aligned bottom cell is 0.
- Demo 2: 23x15 split by full row 12 (color 6) into two 11x15 panels. Top sparse color-9 cells and bottom sparse color-3 cells overlap at only local row 6, col 11; output is 11x15 with a single 2 there.
- Accepted test: 4x9 split by full column 5 (color 1) into two 4x4 panels. Output is [[0,0,0,2],[0,2,2,0],[0,0,0,0],[0,2,0,0]], exactly the nonzero/nonzero overlaps.
- Additional accepted case: 27x29 split by full column 15 (color 6) into two 27x14 panels; left has sparse 9s, right sparse 0/7 with 7 as occupied. Output is 27x14, color 2 precisely at local cells where left and right are both nonzero, otherwise 0. Confirms this task variant treats any nonzero color in each panel as occupied and supports horizontal panel alignment over a tall grid.

## Recurring task ID may vary by instance
Task-9a9d9fc4 has also appeared with a 28x5 demo split by a full column (separator color 7) into two 28x2 panels. In that demo, the output is 3 where the aligned input cells are exactly equal, and 5 otherwise; e.g. row 1 compares left [5,5] with right [5,2] and outputs [3,5]. Do not assume the previously observed background-background variant from task-9a9d9fc4 is universal. Re-derive the cellwise rule from each instance's demos. For a new test of this equality variant, use literal equality of aligned panel cells, not background classification. Check panel boundaries carefully: the separator must be excluded, and the two panels are immediately adjacent to it.

## Verified task-9a9d9fc4 variant: literal equality, marker 3 / fallback 0
A demo pair established a full horizontal separator row (color 4), with two 10x8 panels above and below it. The upper panel uses colors 6/7 and the lower panel uses 7/8. Output is panel-sized: color 3 exactly where aligned cells are literally equal, and 0 otherwise. The output demo marks only equal 7/7 intersections (including cases where one or both are not dominant/background values); it is not a background-only overlap and not non-background occupancy. Test input with separator color 6, upper panel colors 0/9, lower panel colors 0/4 was accepted using the same literal equality rule: output 3 for equality, 0 for mismatch. Exclude the separator and align the 12 rows above with the 12 rows below it.

## Additional verified task-9a9d9fc4 variants
- Another instance of this recurring task ID used a full vertical separator column (color 0) splitting a 9x19 input into two 9x9 panels. Two demos established output 3 exactly where corresponding cells were literally equal, and mismatch/background color 8 otherwise. Demo 1 had equality 8/8 at rows 2, 6, 8, 10, 11 and 9/9 at rows 12-13, etc.; outputs mark equality positions with 3 and all mismatches as 8. Demo 2, a 5x15 grid split into 5x7 panels by column 8, output 3 at equal pairs and 4 otherwise. Thus the output uses literal equality with marker 3; mismatch color is the dominant/background color of the *left panel* (demo 1 left 8, demo 2 left 4). For test with panels full of 9s and sparse 7s on left and 5s on right, accepted output was 3 where left and right cells match exactly, otherwise 9. This confirms infer mismatch color from left panel's background, not the right panel's background or a fixed color. Carefully exclude separator and compare immediate panels cell-for-cell.

## Additional verified task-9a9d9fc4 variants
- Another vertical-split instance (29x13, separator column 7, panels 29x6) used literal equality: output 3 where aligned cells in the two panels were equal, and output 8 otherwise. The shared noise color 8 in the panels was the mismatch/background output, not the dominant panel backgrounds. This candidate was accepted after earlier attempts using background-background/other fallback rules were rejected.
- A 15x7 demo with separator column 4 established equality-marker behavior as output 3 on equal cells and 0 otherwise. A separate demo in another instance had equality marked 3 and mismatch 5. Thus both output colors are instance-dependent; infer exact color mapping from demos rather than assuming panel backgrounds or a fixed mismatch color.

## Validation pitfalls
- Compare corresponding local coordinates, not neighboring positions or mirrored coordinates.
- Treat every nonzero panel color as occupied; do not require colors to match.
- Output zero if either side is zero; mark 2 only for nonzero/nonzero overlap.
- Exclude separator and ensure output is exactly one panel's dimensions.

# ARC prototype stamping

Use this pattern when an ARC grid has a repeated background, several isolated same-color marker cells, and one compact non-background prototype shape.

1. Identify the background color, isolated markers, prototype bounding box, and prototype motif.
2. Infer the prototype's anchor relative to each marker. In the observed task, the marker occupied the prototype's center cell.
3. Copy the prototype's non-background cells around every marker with the same relative offsets. Treat prototype-background cells as transparent; preserve the destination background rather than stamping the prototype background.
4. Replace each marker with the prototype's center/anchor value; retain the original prototype if the pattern indicates it remains in place.
5. Some tasks use the prototype itself as a motif to clone wherever that exact colored-cell silhouette fits entirely on an eligible destination color, rather than singleton markers as anchors. Infer the eligible destination color from the demo; do not assume it is the most common/background-looking color. In one demonstrated variant, the dominant field was 9, sparse cells were 0, and copies were stamped only where every prototype-colored offset landed on 0; the 9 cells were preserved. Search translations of the prototype's non-background offsets over the demonstrated eligible color, paint those cells with the prototype color, and keep the original. This applies to arbitrary motifs, not only straight lines: use every cell of the prototype color in its bounding box as offsets. Do not require the prototype's background-colored cells to match; they are transparent. Paint the union of all valid translations, including overlapping placements, while preserving every non-eligible destination cell. For a straight 3-cell line prototype, this means every eligible-color translated run of length three. The same rule applies to asymmetric motifs such as an L: derive the exact occupied offsets from the prototype and match all those offsets against the eligible color; do not require the motif's bounding-box gaps to match. For example, a 2x2 L prototype with occupied offsets at top-left, top-right, and bottom-left stamps at every translation where all three cells are eligible, painting their union while preserving all other cells. Be careful to use the demonstrated motif orientation and preserve all non-target cells.

7. Coordinate translation and motif orientation are easy to get wrong. Derive offsets directly from the colored prototype cells relative to its bounding-box top-left, then slide the shape through the grid at every in-bounds top-left. Validate the rule against the demo by comparing the union of predicted translated cells with exactly the cells that changed from background to motif color. This catches wrong offsets and wrong fill-color/background assumptions before applying it to a test.
6. Check all placements remain within grid bounds and don't overwrite unrelated structures, then submit the full output grid.

Observed example: a 3x3 motif was propagated centered on each singleton marker, with background-colored prototype cells transparent. Verify anchor and transparency from each new task's demo rather than assuming every prototype is centered.

## Edge-striped ray propagation variant
When a grid has colored bars on opposite outer edges (e.g. left edge at top, right edge at bottom), plus sparse marker cells of a separate color, demos may show rays extending horizontally from the side stripe toward the opposite side on rows with markers. Preserve edge bars and unrelated background. The marker becomes an accent color (in examples, 2 becomes 4), while intervening cells take the edge-stripe color. A marker may not lie directly on a stripe-colored row: first infer from examples whether the nearest stripe, same-side stripe, or marker-defined region controls propagation. Do not infer a universal fill for all rows: examples include partial vertical bar expansion where a stripe's run extends through much of the grid but is interrupted by other features. Validate exact direction, extent, and whether the far edge cell changes against all demos. In a demonstrated case, top-left and bottom-right edge bars colored 0 seeded straight downward/rightward filling bands in their columns/rows, and each isolated 2 emitted a horizontal fill ray to the right with the marker changed to 4. Similar test instance had left-top and right-bottom bars both color 5, and lower-right markers 2; rows containing markers were filled with 2 toward the far side, each marker changed to 4, with the far-right 5 retained. An earlier attempted rule that filled all cells of the top-left stripe rows with marker color was wrong; preserve those rows absent explicit evidence.

## Connected line boundaries and edge cavities
Some puzzles show one or more connected orthogonal line arrangements rather than separate closed frames. Use demonstrations to identify rectangular cavities defined by horizontal/vertical line segments; a grid edge may function as the missing side of a cavity. Fill only the demonstrated interior cells with the demonstrated fill color, preserving all linework and unrelated regions. # Decode separator-intersection lattices

Use when a large ARC grid has regular horizontal/vertical separator lines with mostly uniform background along the lines, while small colored values appear at crossings. The output may be a compressed matrix over adjacent lattice faces.

## Verified evidence from task-47246f29

Three supplied demonstrations decode exactly by reading colored values at successive separator intersections. For each output cell, inspect the four corner crossing values from a 2x2 block of adjacent intersections: if all four crossing values are the same, output that color; otherwise output the interior panel/background color (3 in the demonstrated examples).

Demo 3 gives a clear cell-by-cell check. Lattice crossing rows are 8,13,18,23,28 and columns 4,9,14,19,24,29. Output is the 4x5 matrix for adjacent pairs of crossing rows/columns. E.g. the top-left 2x2 crossing block is all 0, so output 0; the next is all 0; mixed corners map to panel background 3; the bottom-right all-4 block maps to 4. This reproduces all 20 output cells. Demo 1 similarly produces a 4x6 matrix; demo 2's all-uniform lattice decodes to a single 8.

## Region selection resolved on task-47246f29

Do not assume a universal marker-only crop rule. Form faces between consecutive separator-crossing rows and columns, but use demos to determine the lattice span and whether edge crossings are included. Mixed corner colors map to the panel/interior background; unanimous four corners map to that shared color.

Fresh demo/test sequence validates full edge-inclusive lattice extent. Demo grid 27x23 had horizontal separator rows 1,4,7,10,13,16,19,22,25 and vertical separator columns 1,8,15,22. Crop crossings to rows 4..22 and cols 1..22, yielding 6x3 faces, with mixed cells becoming background 8. Test grid 24x28 had separator rows 0,5,10,15,20 and columns 0,6,12,18,24. The edge-inclusive lattice produced 4x4 faces, mixed cells background 2, and unanimous corners copied. Accepted output:
`[[2,2,2,7],[6,2,2,2],[2,2,2,2],[2,1,2,8]]`.

Older examples for this task showed other marker-based cropping; treat crop boundaries as instance-dependent and infer them from geometry plus demos, rather than assuming standout marker colors alone define the span.

## Method

1. Locate repeating full separator rows/columns and list their intersection coordinates.
2. Derive candidate output dimensions from adjacent intersections/faces, but test whether boundary rows/columns are clipped or only a subset is selected.
3. For each candidate face, read its four crossing colors. Compare uniform corners versus mixed corners; mixed faces may map to the panel background.
4. Replay the entire candidate output against every demo, including dimensions, before applying it.
5. If a test disagrees despite exact demo replay, treat it as evidence of an unmodeled selection or clipping rule; do not repeat near-identical outputs. Strict action interface: one JSON action only.
